item.text:
Continuation research completed across all eight selected chapters. No scores, ranges, anchors, or ranking advice assigned.

Persistence remains unavailable: the worker cannot read or write the repository, so `research-ledger-manifest.json` could not be updated here. The following manifest-ready additions use globally new IDs `E031–E043`; existing `E001–E030` should remain unchanged.

### New evidence units

#### 1B — catastrophic-risk governance

- **E031 — 2022 nuclear-risk restraint channel.** SIPRI Yearbook 2023 states that the P5 joint statement affirming that nuclear war cannot be won was issued early in 2022, but Russia’s invasion produced major setbacks in nuclear-arms-control engagement. Most New START elements continued in 2022, while Russia did not resume on-site inspections. Period fit: 2022. Attribution: Russia’s state-level conduct; Putin-level attribution only through presidential control of strategic policy, not personal handling of inspections. Contrary evidence: continued implementation of most treaty elements and the P5 restraint statement. Methodology IDs: `1B.4`, `1B.5`, `1B.7`, `1B.8`, `1B.10`.  
  Source: [SIPRI Yearbook 2023, chapter 8, lines 77–85](https://www.sipri.org/yearbook/2023/08).

- **E032 — nuclear command-and-control interpretation.** Chatham House records Putin’s 27 February order placing Russian nuclear forces on “special mode of combat duty” and explains expert interpretations that this affected launch-command protocols. It also records the uncertainty of technical interpretation and the continued operation of nuclear risk-reduction notification channels. Period fit: February–September 2022. Attribution: direct for Putin’s order; technical effects remain expert interpretation. Contrary evidence: no nuclear weapon was used and normal notification channels remained active for at least some missile activity. Methodology IDs: `1B.2`, `1B.3`, `1B.5`, `1B.6`, `1B.7`, `1B.8`, `1B.9`, `1B.10`.  
  Source: [Chatham House, lines 422–430 and 446–455](https://www.chathamhouse.org/2022/03/how-likely-use-nuclear-weapons-russia).

#### 2B — peace, conflict, and security

- **E033 — humanitarian-corridor and negotiation attempt.** A contemporaneous account records that Russian and Ukrainian delegations agreed in March 2022 to organize humanitarian corridors, while making no progress toward ending the war. This preserves a contrary peace-policy/action unit without treating the announcement as proof of reliable implementation. Period fit: March 2022. Attribution: Russian negotiating position and state conduct; Putin’s personal deliberation is not established. Contrary evidence: Russian demands remained expansive, and humanitarian implementation was contested. Methodology IDs: `2B.3`, `2B.4`, `2B.5`, `2B.7`, `2B.8`, `2B.9`, `2B.10`.  
  Source: [Axios, 3 March 2022](https://www.axios.com/2022/03/03/russia-ukraine-peace-talks-belarus).

- **E034 — proxy-control evidence lead, bounded attribution.** Contemporary reporting records Yevgeny Prigozhin’s September 2022 admission that he founded Wagner and describes the group as serving Kremlin interests. This supports a proxy-control lead and formal network attribution, but not proof that Putin personally directed each Wagner operation. Period fit: 2022. Contrary evidence: Wagner operated through deniable and informal structures, and the available report does not establish Putin’s operational orders. Methodology IDs: `2B.1`, `2B.2`, `2B.4`, `2B.5`, `2B.7`, `2B.8`, `2B.9`, `2B.10`.  
  Source: [The Guardian, 1 November 2022](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/nov/01/russias-wagner-group-have-as-much-power-in-kremlin-as-ministers).

#### 3B — physical integrity and human rights

- **E035 — domestic torture and prison conditions.** The U.S. Department of State’s 2022 Russia report records credible allegations of pervasive law-enforcement torture, harsh and life-threatening prison conditions, arbitrary detention, and lack of accountability. It also records violence and discrimination affecting LGBTQI persons, ethnic and religious minorities, and people with disabilities. Period fit: 2022 report covering the target year. Attribution: government-system and local-authority responsibility; not proof that Putin personally ordered individual abuses. Contrary evidence: the report distinguishes allegations and reported conditions from adjudicated findings and does not establish uniformity across all regions. Methodology IDs: `3B.1`, `3B.2`, `3B.3`, `3B.4`, `3B.5`, `3B.6`, `3B.7`, `3B.8`, `3B.9`, `3B.10`.  
  Source: [U.S. Department of State 2022 Country Report, lines 43–50](https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2089062.html).

- **E036 — political-prisoner treatment and limited remedy.** Amnesty reported in September 2022 that Navalny was repeatedly placed in punishment cells, denied confidential lawyer communication, isolated from other prisoners, and subjected to conditions it characterized as cruel, inhuman, or degrading. Period fit: June–September 2022. Attribution: direct to prison administration; formal presidential responsibility for the national framework is plausible, but personal direction is unproven. Contrary evidence: Amnesty’s account relies partly on lawyers and human-rights sources and is not an adjudicated finding against Putin. Methodology IDs: `3B.1`, `3B.2`, `3B.5`, `3B.7`, `3B.8`, `3B.9`, `3B.10`.  
  Source: [Amnesty International, 16 September 2022, lines 61–76](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2022/09/russia-prison-administration-imposes-harsh-conditions-on-aleksei-navalny/).

- **E037 — vulnerable civilians and torture in occupied areas.** Amnesty documented forcible transfers of older people and people with disabilities, abusive filtration procedures, and seven cases of torture or other ill-treatment of civilians detained by Russian forces. Period fit: March–November 2022. Attribution: Russian forces and occupation structures; this does not prove Putin personally ordered each incident. Contrary evidence: the evidence is case-based and does not establish a population-wide rate. Methodology IDs: `3B.1`, `3B.2`, `3B.3`, `3B.4`, `3B.6`, `3B.7`, `3B.8`, `3B.9`, `3B.10`.  
  Source: [Amnesty International, 7 November 2022, lines 97–115](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2022/11/ukraine-russias-unlawful-transfer-of-civilians-a-war-crime-and-likely-a-crime-against-humanity-new-report/).

#### 4B — political freedom and institutional checks

- **E038 — 2022 regional elections and competitiveness.** OSW reports that September 2022 regional and municipal elections produced victories for Kremlin-backed candidates, that independent monitoring group Golos assessed competitiveness as the lowest since 2012, and that candidate registration, campaigning, and voting were subject to comprehensive official control. Period fit: September 2022. Attribution: institutional and Kremlin-aligned political control; it does not establish Putin’s personal intervention in each election. Contrary evidence: elections were formally held, multiple regions participated, and official results provide a competing account of legitimacy. Methodology IDs: `4B.1`, `4B.2`, `4B.3`, `4B.4`, `4B.5`, `4B.6`, `4B.7`, `4B.8`, `4B.9`, `4B.10`.  
  Source: [OSW, 15 September 2022, lines 48–64](https://www.osw.waw.pl/en/publikacje/analyses/2022-09-15/russia-regional-pseudo-elections-shadow-war).

- **E039 — digital surveillance and mobilization enforcement.** Human Rights Watch reported that Moscow authorities used facial-recognition surveillance to identify and detain alleged draft evaders and anti-mobilization protesters in October 2022, with weak legal safeguards and documented false positives. Period fit: October 2022. Attribution: Moscow police and state surveillance system; federal presidential responsibility is indirect through the national mobilization framework and security policy. Contrary evidence: the report documents a limited number of cases and does not establish the system’s full national reach. Methodology IDs: `4B.2`, `4B.3`, `4B.5`, `4B.6`, `4B.7`, `4B.8`, `4B.9`, `4B.10`.  
  Source: [Human Rights Watch, 26 October 2022, lines 605–613](https://www.hrw.org/news/2022/10/26/russia-uses-facial-recognition-hunt-down-draft-evaders).

#### 5B — economic governance and distribution

- **E040 — distributional and capture context.** The World Bank’s Russia Systematic Country Diagnostic identifies wealth inequality and unequal distribution of productive assets as risks to competition and wealth capture. It also records that education, health, transfers, and pensions reduced measured inequality, while noting that the figures relied on older data rather than 2022 outcomes. Period fit: persistent baseline relevant to 2022, not a target-year event. Attribution: national institutional context, not personalized ruler evidence. Contrary evidence: fiscal transfers and in-kind services had redistributive effects. Methodology IDs: `5B.2`, `5B.3`, `5B.4`, `5B.5`, `5B.6`, `5B.7`, `5B.8`, `5B.9`, `5B.10`.  
  Source: [World Bank Russia SCD, PDF pp. 136–137, lines 4606–4647](https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/477441484190095052/pdf/FINAL-Russia-SCD-Dec-22-ENG-12222016.pdf).

- **E041 — formal public-program audit framework.** Russia’s Accounts Chamber adopted a methodology in March 2022 for evaluating the formation and implementation quality of state programs during subsequent federal-budget control. This establishes an institutional correction and audit mechanism, but does not show whether a specific 2022 program passed review or whether Putin used the mechanism to correct failures. Period fit: March 2022. Attribution: formal state institutional framework; no personal effectiveness inference. Contrary evidence: methodological capacity is not outcome evidence. Methodology IDs: `5B.5`, `5B.6`, `5B.8`, `5B.9`, `5B.10`.  
  Source: [Russian Accounts Chamber methodology, lines 15–33](https://www.consultant.ru/document/cons_doc_LAW_416706/).

#### 6B — health, education, and social provision

- **E042 — federal delivery architecture and intended coverage.** A Russian government report describes 2022 initiatives in health, education, social assistance, infection-control infrastructure, and a “Social Treasury” model intended to extend support to families, disabled people, and older people. This is evidence of policy scope and intended delivery, not independent effectiveness. Period fit: 2022 agenda. Attribution: federal executive policy under presidential system; implementation remained partly regional. Contrary evidence: the source is official and aspirational, with no independent outcome audit. Methodology IDs: `6B.1`, `6B.2`, `6B.3`, `6B.4`, `6B.5`, `6B.6`, `6B.7`, `6B.8`, `6B.9`, `6B.10`.  
  Source: [Russian Government 2022 agenda](https://government.ru/en/news/44452/).

- **E043 — regional and distributional measurement limitation.** Rosstat’s health-statistics program states that health information is collected from agencies, households, and federal surveys, with regional data supplied separately. This supports the existence of a measurement infrastructure for regional variation, but the accessible record does not itself establish 2022 service quality, equity, or improvement. Period fit: target-period statistical system; substantive data year requires verification in the underlying 2023 publication. Attribution: none to Putin beyond national administrative responsibility. Contrary evidence: data collection and regional disaggregation provide a potential corrective mechanism. Methodology IDs: `6B.3`, `6B.4`, `6B.5`, `6B.7`, `6B.8`, `6B.9`, `6B.10`.  
  Source: [Rosstat health-statistics publication page](https://www.rosstat.gov.ru/folder/210/document/13218).

#### 7B — personal integrity and corruption

- **E044 — documented assets of Putin-linked networks, not personal proof.** The UK government’s May 2022 sanctions notice identifies family members, financiers, and associates in Putin’s inner circle and explains the legal effects of asset freezes. OCCRP’s Russian Asset Tracker, updated through August 2022, documents more than $19.8 billion in assets linked through documentary evidence to wealthy and powerful Russians, including properties linked to Putin associates. These sources support a network/integrity lead, not a verified finding that Putin personally owned or controlled the assets. Period fit: 2022 sanctions and tracker update. Contrary evidence: official Russian asset declarations and denials remain unresolved; no adjudicated finding against Putin was located. Methodology IDs: `7B.1`, `7B.2`, `7B.3`, `7B.4`, `7B.5`, `7B.6`, `7B.7`, `7B.8`, `7B.9`, `7B.10`.  
  Sources: [UK sanctions notice, lines 121–139 and 156](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-sanctions-the-shady-network-funding-putins-lavish-lifestyle); [OCCRP Russian Asset Tracker, lines 42–45 and 119–130](https://www.occrp.org/en/project/russian-asset-tracker).

#### 8B — effectiveness and governing capacity

- **E045 — mobilization implementation failure and correction claim.** Axios reported that Russia’s September 2022 mobilization generated administrative errors, protest, disproportionate exposure of rural and ethnic-minority populations, and very short training periods; Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the errors would be corrected. Period fit: September 2022. Attribution: direct presidential mobilization authority, with implementation delegated to state and regional bodies. Contrary evidence: the “errors will be corrected” statement is an official corrective claim without independent verification. Methodology IDs: `8B.1`, `8B.2`, `8B.3`, `8B.4`, `8B.5`, `8B.6`, `8B.7`, `8B.8`, `8B.9`, `8B.10`.  
  Source: [Axios, 27 September 2022, lines 55–70](https://www.axios.com/2022/09/27/russia-mobilization-centers-protests-errors).

- **E046 — institutional effectiveness constraint.** The Accounts Chamber methodology provides evidence that Russia maintained a formal mechanism for evaluating state-program formation and implementation. This is an institutional-capacity fact, not proof that programs were effective or durable. Period fit: March 2022 and persistent through the target period. Attribution: state institutional architecture, not Putin’s personal performance. Contrary evidence: no accessible target-year audit result was located during this pass. Methodology IDs: `8B.2`, `8B.3`, `8B.4`, `8B.5`, `8B.6`, `8B.7`, `8B.8`, `8B.9`, `8B.10`.  
  Source: [Accounts Chamber methodology](https://www.consultant.ru/document/cons_doc_LAW_416706/).

### Search dispositions

- **Accepted:** `E031–E046` above, subject to the stated attribution and period-fit limits.
- **Discovery-only / rejected as standalone evidence:** general 2022 Rosstat publication landing pages without retrievable target-year tables; CSIS proxy-control material because the underlying page was inaccessible; Russian official Bucha and biological-risk claims where the source itself contained contested allegations rather than findings; broad World Bank baseline material where the figures predated 2022.
- **No recoverable evidence found:** Putin’s internal nuclear deliberations, detailed launch authorization practice, independent verification of command-system implementation, verified personal ownership of alleged assets, target-year independent health/education effectiveness audits, and reliable evidence of federal correction after mobilization failures.

### Bias and reconciliation updates

The continuation improves coverage of:

- favorable and contrary peace-policy evidence;
- proxy control without overclaiming personal command;
- prison, torture, vulnerable-group, and remedy gaps;
- elections, courts, local political control, and digital surveillance;
- institutional audit mechanisms and distributional baselines;
- mobilization implementation failures and official correction claims;
- personal-integrity network evidence while preserving allegation status.

Remaining evidence shortfalls are material in 1B, 5B, 6B, 7B, and 8B. Missing evidence remains an uncertainty and attribution limitation, not negative ruler evidence. Duplicate families should be reconciled downstream, especially SIPRI/arms-control items, Human Rights Watch/Amnesty civil-liberties items, and the OCCRP/UK network-asset items.
